    Phase 6a review fixes: fuzzy evidence never grounds an allow; bounded disguise scanning
    
    - from() in an allow rule or a declassify condition counts only deterministic evidence (exact,
      normalized, decoded); fuzzy similarity could otherwise satisfy a declassify and lift the trifecta
      invariant (owner decision 3). Deny/ask rules still use every matcher. Regression test proven to
      fail without the fix.
    - Disguise-undone scanning is bounded per definition (64 KiB of model-visible text); a larger
      definition is reported unscannable (medium, hidden by default). A hostile 2 MB definition took
      ~3.5 s to list; now ~0.2 s (the raw scan), and ~125 ms worst case under the bound.
    - ReDoS checks extended to the new separator regexes; the timing test measures single decoder
      passes (backtracking) rather than variant volume.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

name: ci

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  secret-scan:
    name: secret scan (gitleaks, full history)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    env:
      GITLEAKS_VERSION: 8.30.1
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
          persist-credentials: false
      - name: download gitleaks and verify its checksum
        run: |
          base="https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks/releases/download/v${GITLEAKS_VERSION}"
          tarball="gitleaks_${GITLEAKS_VERSION}_linux_x64.tar.gz"
          curl -fsSLO "$base/$tarball"
          curl -fsSLO "$base/gitleaks_${GITLEAKS_VERSION}_checksums.txt"
          grep " $tarball\$" "gitleaks_${GITLEAKS_VERSION}_checksums.txt" | sha256sum -c -
          mkdir -p "$RUNNER_TEMP/gitleaks" && tar -xzf "$tarball" -C "$RUNNER_TEMP/gitleaks" gitleaks
      - name: scan every commit
        run: '"$RUNNER_TEMP/gitleaks/gitleaks" git --log-opts="--all" --redact --exit-code 1 .'

  test:
    name: ${{ matrix.os }} / node ${{ matrix.node }}
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    timeout-minutes: 30
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest]
        node: [22, 24]
    steps:
      # Actions pinned to commit SHAs (tag in the comment) so a moved tag cannot change what runs.
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-node@949feb2413d6458794dcd2491c4babbbce0c15c1 # v7.1.0
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
          cache: npm
      # --ignore-scripts: dependencies never run install scripts in CI (supply-chain hygiene). It also
      # avoids npm 10 running node-gyp on better-sqlite3, which ships prebuilt binaries in its tarball.
      - run: npm ci --ignore-scripts
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm run typecheck
      - run: npm run build
      - run: npm test
      - name: e2e against the built package
        run: npx vitest run test/cli.e2e.test.ts
        env:
          MCPHANTOM_E2E_DIST: '1'
      - name: tier-1 static scanner benchmark (fails if the held-out split regresses)
        run: npm run bench:scanner
      - name: tier-1 evasion benchmark (fails if a claimed evasion is missed or a benign pair is attributed)
        run: npm run bench:evasion
      - name: install smoke test (packed tarball, fresh prefix)
        shell: bash
        run: |
          npm pack --silent
          prefix="$RUNNER_TEMP/mcphantom-prefix"
          npm install -g --prefix "$prefix" ./mcphantom-*.tgz
          if [ "$RUNNER_OS" = "Windows" ]; then bin="$prefix/mcphantom.cmd"; else bin="$prefix/bin/mcphantom"; fi
          "$bin" --version
          "$bin" doctor

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  render:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    env:
      VHS_VERSION: 0.12.1
      VHS_SHA256: eb33787a5b1cebf91fe0b18bd231e2d71d36c1ff4babd99ddac1a6ab411efd10
      TTYD_VERSION: 1.7.7
      TTYD_SHA256: 8a217c968aba172e0dbf3f34447218dc015bc4d5e59bf51db2f2cd12b7be4f55
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-node@949feb2413d6458794dcd2491c4babbbce0c15c1 # v7.1.0
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci --ignore-scripts
      - run: npm run build
      - run: npm link
      # Binaries pinned by SHA-256 in this file, so a replaced release asset fails the job.
      - name: install vhs, ttyd and ffmpeg
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update -qq && sudo apt-get install -y -qq ffmpeg
          mkdir -p "$RUNNER_TEMP/bin"
          curl -fsSL -o "$RUNNER_TEMP/bin/ttyd" "https://github.com/tsl0922/ttyd/releases/download/${TTYD_VERSION}/ttyd.x86_64"
          echo "${TTYD_SHA256}  $RUNNER_TEMP/bin/ttyd" | sha256sum -c -
          chmod +x "$RUNNER_TEMP/bin/ttyd"
          tarball="vhs_${VHS_VERSION}_Linux_x86_64.tar.gz"
          curl -fsSLO "https://github.com/charmbracelet/vhs/releases/download/v${VHS_VERSION}/${tarball}"
          echo "${VHS_SHA256}  ${tarball}" | sha256sum -c -
          tar -xzf "$tarball" -C "$RUNNER_TEMP" && find "$RUNNER_TEMP" -name vhs -type f -exec mv {} "$RUNNER_TEMP/bin/vhs" \;
          rm -f "$tarball"
          echo "$RUNNER_TEMP/bin" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"
      - run: vhs docs/demo/demo.tape
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@043fb46d1a93c77aae656e7c1c64a875d1fc6a0a # v7.0.1

# MCPhantom — Design

Status: **approved with changes (2026-10-12)**. This document is the source of truth for scope and
sequencing; deviations are recorded in the "Change log" at the end.

MCPhantom is a security gateway that sits between an LLM agent's MCP client and the MCP servers it
uses. It scans and pins tool definitions, tracks the provenance of data flowing through tool calls,
and enforces a declarative per-tool policy — including across the LLM boundary, where data is
paraphrased rather than copied.

---

## 1. Architecture

```
 ┌─────────────┐        stdio          ┌──────────────────────────── MCPhantom gateway ─────────────────────────┐
 │ MCP client  │◄─────────────────────►│ Downstream face (MCP Server, official SDK)                               │
 │ Claude Code │                       │     │                                                                    │
 │ Desktop,    │                       │ ┌───▼──────────── Interception pipeline ───────────────────────────────┐ │
 │ Cursor, ... │                       │ │ 1 Definition gate  pin check (rug-pull) + scanner verdict            │ │
 └─────────────┘                       │ │                    → filters tools/list BEFORE the LLM sees it       │ │
                                       │ │ 2 Call gate        policy: context labels + arg provenance           │ │
                                       │ │                    → allow / ask / deny                               │ │
                                       │ │ 3 Output gate      labels, secret + injection scan, provenance index │ │
                                       │ └───┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
                                       │     │     Session store (labels, bounded provenance index)              │
                                       │ Upstream face (one MCP Client per server)   Event log (SQLite, redacted) │
                                       └─────┼────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────┘
                                             ▼  stdio / HTTP  ▼                             ▼ SSE (loopback)
                                        server A          server B                   Dashboard
```

### Deployment: gateway mode only (v1)

The client config contains a single `mcphantom` entry. MCPhantom spawns/connects every upstream
server listed in its own config and exposes their tools as `<serverId>__<tool>`. Gateway mode is the
only mode in which one process observes every tool call of a session, which cross-server taint
tracking requires. **Wrap mode (per-server shims + daemon) is deferred to a later release.**

- Downstream transport (client → MCPhantom): stdio. (Streamable HTTP downstream is a later addition.)
- Upstream transports (MCPhantom → servers): stdio and Streamable HTTP.
- `mcphantom init` discovers client configs (Claude Code project `.mcp.json`, Claude Desktop,
  Cursor), moves their server entries into the MCPhantom config, replaces them with one `mcphantom`
  entry, shows a diff, writes a backup, and offers bulk classification suggestions (see §3.4).
  `mcphantom uninstall` restores the backup. Paths are resolved per-OS; Windows is first-class.

### Protocol handling rules

- Every method the gateway serves has an explicit handler; it never forwards raw JSON-RPC blindly.
  Handled: `initialize`, `ping`, `tools/list|call`, `resources/list|read|templates/list|subscribe|unsubscribe`,
  `prompts/list|get`, `completion/complete`, `logging/setLevel`; notifications for list changes,
  progress, cancellation, logging, resource updates. **Unknown methods are rejected** (MethodNotFound).
- `tools/list` (and the other list methods) are fully paginated upstream by the gateway — every page
  is fetched and inspected — and returned downstream as one result, bounded by a hard cap.
- Server→client requests: `roots/list` and `elicitation/create` are relayed; **`sampling/createMessage`
  is denied by default** (it lets a server inject text straight into the model) and can be enabled
  per server.
- Experimental `tasks` are not advertised in v1.
- **Fail closed**: an internal error in any gate denies the request and logs the cause.
- Server-provided annotations (`readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`, `openWorldHint`, …) are
  attacker-controlled. They may *tighten* a classification or seed `init` suggestions; they never
  loosen policy.
- Poisoning is stopped at list time: a flagged or unpinned tool is removed from `tools/list`, since
  a description injects into the model the moment it is listed. The server's `instructions` field in
  the `initialize` result is scanned and pinned the same way.

### MCPhantom's own storage is attack surface

| Asset | Protection |
|---|---|
| Event log (SQLite DB + WAL/SHM) | Payloads pass through the secret redactor **before** being written. `log_payloads: redacted (default) \| none \| full`. Retention by age and size (`retention.days`, `retention.max_mb`), pruned at startup and hourly. |
| DB, lockfile, policy, config | POSIX: directory `0700`, files `0600`, created with a restrictive umask. Windows: inheritance removed and a single full-control ACE for the current user's SID (`icacls /inheritance:r /grant:r *<SID>:(OI)(CI)F` on the directory, `(F)` on files) — the 0600 equivalent. Checked at startup; MCPhantom refuses to start (or warns, configurable) if the files are group/world accessible. Covered by CI on Windows, macOS and Linux. |
| Dashboard | Loopback bind, random per-run token, Host-header allowlist (anti-DNS-rebinding), Origin/CSRF checks, strict CSP, tool output rendered as text only. |

**Same-user tampering (threat model entry).** Upstream stdio servers run as the same OS user as
MCPhantom. File permissions do not stop a same-user process from rewriting the lockfile or policy.
Mitigations, in decreasing strength — none is a real boundary:

1. Lockfile and policy are read once at startup; changes made while MCPhantom runs are ignored until
   the next restart (there is no live reload). A tampering server must therefore win a race before the
   next restart, and a changed definition shows up in `mcphantom lock diff`. *(Corrected in Phase 6.5:
   an earlier version described a CLI reload with a diff, which does not exist.)*
2. The lockfile carries an HMAC-SHA256 over its canonical contents, keyed by a 32-byte secret in an
   owner-only key file (`hmac.key`, POSIX `0600` / Windows single-SID ACL). **What this protects:**
   other OS users cannot forge or silently edit the lockfile (they cannot read the key), and accidental
   corruption or truncation is detected. **What it does not protect:** a process running as the *same*
   user — including a malicious MCP server, the attacker already in the threat model — can read the key
   file and re-sign. An OS credential store (DPAPI/Keychain/libsecret) would not change this: its
   CurrentUser scope is reachable by any same-user code, so it offers no additional guarantee against
   the same-user attacker while adding native dependencies. We therefore use an owner-only key file and
   state its scope precisely rather than implying more.
3. Project lockfiles can be committed to git so that changes are code-reviewed.

The real boundary is running upstream servers under a different OS user, in a container, or in a
sandbox. The docs say so plainly.

## 2. Taint tracking across the LLM boundary

MCPhantom sees tool outputs entering the model and tool arguments leaving it; it never sees the
model's context, its reasoning, or the user's prompt. Nothing in the middle can prove that data did
**not** flow through the model. Two layers with different jobs follow.

### Layer 1 — context labels (sound)

Labels form two lattices: integrity `trusted ⊑ untrusted`, confidentiality
`public ⊑ internal ⊑ secret`. Each output is labeled by policy (per server/tool, optionally per
argument). The session **context label** is the monotone join of everything ingested. Once untrusted
content is in the context, every later call is presumed attacker-steerable, regardless of paraphrase.

**Trifecta invariant (default on):** an `egress` call while the context is both `untrusted` and
`secret` is denied unless a named `declassify` entry allows it. Paraphrase cannot bypass this layer
because it does not inspect content. Its cost is over-tainting, which the policy language and Layer 2
make tolerable without giving up soundness.

### Layer 2 — argument provenance (precise)

For each string leaf of a call's arguments: *which earlier outputs did this come from, by which
matcher, with what confidence?*

| Matcher | Catches |
|---|---|
| Exact substring | verbatim copy |
| Normalized | case, whitespace, NFKC, zero-width, homoglyphs |
| Decoded | base64, hex, URL, HTML entities, `\u` escapes, rot13, reversal, separator spelling (args decoded recursively, bounded depth) |
| Fuzzy | light edits/reordering (winnowing k-gram fingerprints) |
| Cumulative | exfiltration split across many calls (per-sink reassembly) |
| Semantic | paraphrase (local embeddings) — **dropped from v1 (2026-10-13)**: the security-critical parts of an exfiltration are high-entropy identifiers that exact/decoded/cumulative matching attributes; paraphrased low-entropy payloads stay covered by Layer 1. Revisit after v1 only with a measured gain |

**Core insight.** The security-critical parts of an exfiltration — the *destination* (attacker URL,
address) and the *secret* (key, token) — are high-entropy identifiers that must cross the LLM
boundary *exactly* or the attack fails. They are attributable by matchers that hold up under
adversarial pressure (exact/normalized/decoded/cumulative) even when the surrounding prose is
paraphrased. Paraphrase only defeats attribution for low-entropy payloads, which Layer 1 still covers.

**Honesty rule.** Layer-2 evidence may add restrictions, explain a decision, or satisfy an
author-written allow rule (e.g. "recipient not from untrusted"). The absence of a match is never
treated as proof of absence of flow; any policy relying on that gets a "precision-mode, bypassable"
lint warning.

Every server also receives its arguments, so every `tools/call` is egress to that server

# MCPhantom

**A security gateway for MCP that blocks the lethal trifecta even when the model paraphrases. It
measures its own detection and publishes every bypass it knows about.**

![An agent reads a poisoned blog post and tries to send a canary AWS key from .env to an attacker. Without MCPhantom the key reaches the attacker; with MCPhantom the call is blocked and the trace shows why.](docs/demo/demo.gif)

*The verdict in the demo comes from the attacker collector's own request log, not from MCPhantom.
The agent is scripted (no model), so the result shows what the defense does, not what a model happened
to do. Regenerate it: [docs/demo/](docs/demo/).*

> **Status: v0.1, an early release.** Development has been on Windows 11, with CI on Linux, macOS and
> Windows × Node 22/24. Not published to npm yet (planned for v1). Read
> [Known limitations and bypasses](#known-limitations-and-bypasses) before you rely on it.

## What it blocks today

| Threat | What MCPhantom does | Reproduce |
|---|---|---|
| **Lethal-trifecta exfiltration.** Untrusted content steers the agent into sending your secrets out. | Once a session has seen both untrusted and secret data, any `egress`/`exec` call (and any `write` outside its declared workspace) is **denied**. This check never looks at content, so paraphrasing doesn't get past it. | `npm run demo`, `test/demo.e2e.test.ts` |
| **Tool poisoning.** Hidden instructions in tool, prompt or server `instructions` text. | Scanned **before the model sees the list**: invisible Unicode, embedded instructions, shadowing, exfiltration hints, including disguised versions (look-alike characters, base64/hex/URL encoding, letter-spacing, …). A flagged tool is removed from `tools/list`. | `npm run bench:scanner`, `npm run bench:evasion`, `test/scanner.gateway.test.ts` |
| **Rug-pulls.** A definition changes after you approved it. | `mcphantom approve` pins model-visible definitions (canonical JSON + SHA-256, HMAC-signed lockfile). Changed or new definitions are hidden, including ones introduced mid-session via `list_changed`. | `test/rugpull.gateway.test.ts`, `mcphantom lock diff` |
| **Unsafe calls by tool.** | Per-tool [CEL](https://cel.dev) rules: `deny` > `ask` > `allow`, with predicates such as `from(arg.to, "untrusted")` (where did this value come from?), `containsSecret(arg)`, `glob`, `within`. Named, audited `declassify` exceptions. `ask` uses MCP elicitation; on clients without it, `ask` is a deny. | `test/policy.gateway.test.ts`, `mcphantom policy explain` |
| **Server-to-model injection.** | `sampling/createMessage` is denied by default (per-server opt-in). Unknown methods are rejected, and any internal error denies the request (fail-closed). | `test/gateway.test.ts` |

Every decision is recorded with its rule, its sources and its evidence (`mcphantom trace`). Payloads
are redacted *before* they reach the event log.

## Quick start

Requires Node ≥ 22.13 and git. v0.1 runs from a checkout (or from the tarball attached to the
GitHub release):

```sh
git clone https://github.com/Amineddine/mcphantom && cd mcphantom
npm install && npm run build
npm run demo                    # unprotected vs. protected, same poisoned page and attacker
npm link                        # puts `mcphantom` on your PATH
mcphantom trace --last --data-dir "<printed by the demo>"
```

From the release tarball instead: `npm install -g ./mcphantom-0.1.0.tgz`. That gives you the
`mcphantom` CLI; the demo needs a checkout until Phase 9.

Protect your own MCP setup:

```sh
cd your-project
mcphantom init                  # finds .mcp.json / Claude Desktop / Cursor config, shows a diff, asks
mcphantom approve --profile <name>   # pin today's tool definitions (enables rug-pull detection)
mcphantom doctor                # paths, profiles, permission checks
```

`init` moves your MCP servers into an MCPhantom profile and replaces them with a single `mcphantom`
entry. A backup of the original config is kept, and `mcphantom uninstall --profile <name>` restores it.
Tools then appear as `<server>__<tool>`. Until `approve` has been run nothing is pinned, so rug-pull
detection is inactive.

## How it works

```
 MCP client ──stdio──► MCPhantom ─┬─► server A   (stdio or Streamable HTTP)
 (Claude Code,          │         └─► server B
  Desktop, Cursor)      ├─ 1 definition gate   scan + pin check → filters tools/list before the model sees it
                        ├─ 2 call gate         context label + argument provenance + CEL policy → allow / ask / deny
                        └─ 3 output gate       label the output, detect secrets, index it for provenance
```

MCPhantom sees tool outputs entering the model and tool arguments leaving it. It never sees the model's
context or reasoning, so it cannot prove that data did **not** pass through the model. That is why it
works in two layers with different jobs:

- **Layer 1: context labels (sound).** Every output gets an integrity label (`trusted ⊑ untrusted`)
  and a confidentiality label (`public ⊑ internal ⊑ secret`). The session's label only ever rises. Once
  it is both untrusted and secret, egress is denied unless a named `declassify` entry allows it. This
  layer never inspects content, so paraphrase and encoding cannot get around it. The price is
  over-tainting, i.e. false blocks.
- **Layer 2: argument provenance (precise, evidence only).** For each string in a call's arguments,
  MCPhantom asks which earlier output it came from. Matchers: exact, normalized (case, NFKC, zero-width,
  confusables), decoded (base64, hex, URL, entities, escapes, rot13, reversal, separator spelling,
  chains up to depth 3), fuzzy (winnowing fingerprints) and cumulative (a secret split across calls).
  The idea behind it: the parts of an exfiltration that matter, the attacker's address and the secret,
  are high-entropy identifiers that must cross the model *exactly*, or the attack fails.
  **Honesty rule:** Layer-2 evidence can add a restriction, explain a decision, or satisfy an allow rule
  you wrote. Finding no match is never treated as proof that nothing flowed. Allow rules and declassify
  conditions count only deterministic evidence (exact/normalized/decoded), never fuzzy similarity.

Full design, threat model and decisions: [docs/DESIGN.md](docs/DESIGN.md).

## Configuration

Profiles live in the MCPhantom config directory (`%APPDATA%\mcphantom` on Windows,
`~/Library/Application Support/mcphantom` on macOS, `~/.config/mcphantom` on Linux):

```yaml
version: 1
servers:
  web:
    command: uvx
    args: ["mcp-server-fetch"]                   # the reference fetch server
    defaults: { integrity: untrusted }            # a third party controls what it returns
  fs:
    command: npx
    args: ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/work"]
    tools:
      read_file: { effect: read, integrity: trusted }
      write_file: { effect: write, workspace: /work }   # a write outside /work counts as egress
  mail:
    type: http
    url: https://mcp.example.com/mcp
    headers: { Authorization: "Bearer ${TOKEN}" }  # ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default}, as in .mcp.json
    tools:
      send_email:
        effect: egress
        rules:
          - deny: 'from(arg.to, "untrusted")'      # recipient copied from untrusted content
          - deny: 'containsSecret(arg)'
          - ask:  'context.integrity == "untrusted"'
declassify:
  - id: own-inbox
    tool: mail__send_email
    when: 'arg.to == "me@corp.example"'
    reason: "My own inbox; accepted risk"
```

Anything you don't classify is treated as `egress` with `untrusted` output. `mcphantom suggest` proposes
classifications from server annotations and tool names. Those annotations are claims made by the server,
so a suggestion looser than the secure default needs `--accept-loose`. `mcphantom policy lint` checks
your rules against the live tool schemas.

Security-relevant defaults:

| Setting | Default | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `taint.trifecta` | `deny` | `log` is audit mode, which the unprotected half of the demo uses. |
| `scan.block` / `scan.mode` | `medium` / `hide` | Flagged definitions never reach the model. |
| `rugpull.mode` / `on_bad_signature` | `enforce` / `refuse` | A tampered or malformed lockfile stops startup instead of disabling the check. |
| `env_inherit` | `minimal` | Servers get the SDK's small environment allowlist plus their own `env`, never the gateway's full environment. |
| `allow_sampling` | `false` | `sampling/createMessage` lets a server put text straight into the model. |
| `logging.payloads` | `redacted` | Credentials are removed *before* anything is written to disk. |
| `logging.on_failure` | `warn` | `deny` makes the audit log a control: a request (tool call, prompt, resource read or subscription, completion, relayed server request) that can't be logged before it is forwarded is refused, and a result that can't be logged is withheld. |
| `resources.unrouted` | `deny` | A resource URI that no server listed is refused. |
| `security.insecure_permissions` | `fix` | Config, profiles and the event DB are restricted to your user (POSIX `0600`/`0700`; on Windows an ACL with a single entry for your SID). |

# Changelog

## Unreleased

### Fixed

- **A policy `ask` was skipped in trifecta audit mode.** With `taint.trifecta: log`, a call that tripped
  the invariant was allowed without asking, even when a policy rule required confirmation. The `ask`
  now applies; the decision's reason also records the audited invariant. The default
  (`taint.trifecta: deny`) was not affected.
- **`logging.on_failure: deny` now holds before forwarding.** `prompts/get`, `resources/read`,
  `resources/subscribe` and `completion/complete` were sent upstream before anything was audited; only
  the response was withheld. They are now recorded first (`request` event, outcome `forwarding`), and
  not sent if that write fails. The default (`warn`) was not affected beyond the extra event.

## 0.1.0 (2026-10-13)

First public release. Early software: read
[Known limitations and bypasses](README.md#known-limitations-and-bypasses) before relying on it. Not on
npm yet (planned for v1); install from a checkout or from the tarball attached to the GitHub release.

### What's in it

- **Gateway core (Phase 1).** A single `mcphantom` entry in front of your MCP servers. Downstream is
  stdio; upstream is stdio or Streamable HTTP. Tools are namespaced `<server>__<tool>`. Every method has
  an explicit handler, unknown methods are rejected, and failures close (deny). `sampling/createMessage`
  is denied by default, and servers get a minimal environment. Listings and HTTP bodies are byte-bounded
  and redirects stay same-origin. A URI claimed by two servers is unroutable, which prevents resource
  shadowing. There is a redacted SQLite event log with retention, and MCPhantom's own files are
  restricted to your user (POSIX modes, Windows single-SID ACLs). CLI: `init` (Claude Code, Claude
  Desktop, Cursor; shows a diff and keeps a backup), `uninstall`, `run`, `doctor`.
- **Taint tracking and the trifecta invariant (Phase 2).** Integrity and confidentiality labels, and a
  per-connection context label that only rises. An egress/exec call while the context is both untrusted
  and secret is denied; a `write` outside its workspace counts as egress. Exact and normalized argument
  provenance, with a bounded two-tier index. Detected secrets count as a taint source. `mcphantom trace`.
  Deterministic side-by-side demo (`npm run demo`).
- **Static scanner (Phase 3).** Hidden Unicode, embedded instructions, tool shadowing, and
  exfiltration/credential hints in tools, prompts and server `instructions`. Flagged items are hidden at
  list time. Tier-1 benchmark (`npm run bench:scanner`).
- **Rug-pull detection (Phase 4).** Canonical-JSON SHA-256 pins in an HMAC-signed lockfile
  (`mcphantom approve`, `mcphantom lock diff`). Changed or new definitions are hidden, including after
  `list_changed`. A tampered or malformed lockfile stops startup.
- **Policy engine (Phase 5).** Per-tool CEL rules (deny > ask > allow) with `from`, `containsSecret`,
  `glob`, `within`; named, audited `declassify` exceptions; `ask` via MCP elicitation, otherwise deny;
  fail-closed on absent arguments, CEL errors and the evaluation deadline. `policy lint/test/explain`,
  `suggest`.
- **Layer-2 deepening (Phase 6a).** A shared normalize/decode pipeline (Unicode confusables 16.0.0,
  despacing, bounded decoders) feeding the decoded, fuzzy (winnowing) and cumulative (split across calls)
  matchers. The scanner runs through the same pipeline. Allow rules and declassify count only
  deterministic evidence. `logging.on_failure: deny` and `resources.unrouted: deny`. Adversarial-evasion
  benchmark (`npm run bench:evasion`) in CI.

### Measured (deterministic, author-written suites; commands in the README)

- Scanner, held-out split: TPR 100%, FPR 0% (14 poisoned + 41 benign definitions, a small corpus).
- Evasion: 143/143 claimed attribution transformations caught, 0/36 false attributions, 90/90 claimed
  scanner disguises caught. Every evasion that still succeeds is listed in
  `bench/results/evasion-bench.md`.
- Decision latency p50: 1.6 ms (small arguments), 86 ms (128 KB body), on an i5-8250U laptop.

### Known limitations

Client-native tools are not covered. MCPhantom is not a sandbox. Same-user tampering is mitigated, not
prevented. Resources are not pinned. Secret detection has no entropy detector yet. Per-server
`may_receive` is not implemented. `ask` without elicitation is a deny. Full list in the README.

v0.1.0 — first public release

MCPhantom is a security gateway that sits between an MCP client (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor) and your MCP servers. It blocks the lethal trifecta: once a session has seen both untrusted content and secret data, egress is denied, and because that check never looks at content, paraphrasing doesn't get past it. It also hides poisoned or rug-pulled tool definitions before the model sees them and enforces per-tool CEL policy. It measures its own detection and publishes every bypass it knows about.

This is an early release: please read **Known limitations and bypasses** in the README before relying on it.

### Highlights
- Trifecta invariant (Layer 1, content-blind), plus argument provenance (Layer 2): exact, normalized, decoded, fuzzy and cumulative matchers that explain decisions and add restrictions.
- Static scanner at list time (hidden Unicode, embedded instructions, shadowing, exfiltration hints, including disguised versions).
- Rug-pull pinning with an HMAC-signed lockfile (`mcphantom approve`, `lock diff`).
- CEL policy: deny > ask > allow, `from()` / `containsSecret()` / `glob()` / `within()`, audited `declassify`.
- Fail-closed throughout; sampling denied by default; redacted audit log; owner-only file permissions on Windows, macOS and Linux.

### Measured (deterministic, author-written suites)
- Scanner, held-out split: TPR 100%, FPR 0% on 14 poisoned + 41 benign definitions (a small corpus: a regression floor, not a claim about novel attacks).
- Evasion: 143/143 claimed attribution transformations caught, 0/36 false attributions; 90/90 claimed scanner disguises caught. Every evasion that still succeeds is listed in `bench/results/evasion-bench.md`.
- Live-model attack-success rates are not measured yet (Phase 9).

### Install
Not on npm yet (planned for v1). Either clone and build (`npm install && npm run build && npm link`), or install the attached tarball: `npm install -g ./mcphantom-0.1.0.tgz` (Node ≥ 22.13). SHA-256 of the tarball: `da37c96e8698a11a067abbac638a3a67380db84a57b8759b3cb4125df801d1cb` (packed from tag v0.1.0 = 46044d9).

Full changes: CHANGELOG.md. Every phase's hostile review, including the code paths that are not tested: docs/reviews/.

Security reports: private GitHub advisories only (see SECURITY.md).
